lessons.title: Where your data goes
lessons.subtitle: Where a prompt goes before the answer

sections.title: Check product and operation together
sections.content:
Where does your prompt land? Not the brand decides it. Product edition, contract, configuration, workflow do. Six fields:

| Review field | Concrete questions |
|---|---|
| **Roles** | Who is the controller, processor, or another recipient? Is a processing agreement required and in place? |
| **Data flows** | Which content, metadata, and logs leave which system? In which regions are they stored or processed? |
| **Provider use** | Are inputs or outputs used for model development, quality review, or abuse monitoring? Which settings and contractual commitments apply? |
| **Access and functions** | Which roles, permissions, connectors, extensions, and sharing links are active? |
| **Lifecycle** | How long are inputs, outputs, logs, and backups retained? How do access, deletion, and export work? |
| **Organizational approval** | Which purposes, data classes, user groups, and configurations does the approval cover? |

Cloud or local, free or paid, consumer or enterprise: sales categories, not protection classes. A local system sends telemetry, loads extensions, reaches the network. An enterprise contract does not cover every function and data class. Read the current contract and product documentation at procurement and after material changes.
sections.keyTakeaway: Roles, data flows, provider use, access, retention, approved purpose. That is your check. Product category and brand name check nothing.

sections.title: Shadow AI, and what works against it
sections.content:
Shadow AI is any AI use for work that nobody approved. The private chat account is the best-known case. Browser extensions count too, and the new function in long-bought software, the personal API key, the local model outside the process.

An unapproved workflow can lack contract, legal basis, permissions, data region, retention, logging, technical controls. The switch marked "training use off" answers none of that.

What helps has to work in daily life. A current approval matrix, data rules people understand, contacts people reach, a procurement path people can check. Approved alternatives good enough for the task. Add access control, configuration policies, logging or blocks by risk.

And you? Look up the published approval status before any work processing. This purpose, this data class, this product edition, this active configuration.
sections.keyTakeaway: Shadow AI is every AI workflow without approval. Clear approvals, usable alternatives and technical controls lower the risk.

quiz.questionText: Which option is safest for company data?

answerOptions.text: Any free service, because wide adoption counts as approval
An enterprise product approved by IT and data protection, in the reviewed configuration
A service with a European head office, unchecked product and data flows
There is no difference between the tools

quiz.explanation: Safe is what was checked: product, contract, permissions, data classes, tenant and data region. A brand name checks nothing. Nor a European head office.

quiz.questionText: What does "Shadow AI" mean in an organizational context?

answerOptions.text: A particularly secure AI that works in the background
The IT department's use of AI tools
Employees using AI tools without the organization's knowledge or authorization
A privacy feature of a particular chat product

quiz.explanation: An AI workflow nobody approved. A consumer offer, an extension, a personal API key, a local model, a new function in long-bought software.

lessons.title: The four levels of data classification
lessons.subtitle: Which data belongs in which tool

sections.title: Four levels, an example
sections.content:
Your organization sets which data may go into which system. Not this course. The four levels here are an example, no mapping to product names.

**Level 1: Public**
What is already published: approved website copy, the product catalogue. You still check copyright, licences, embedded personal data and the tool approval. Public does not mean free to use.

**Level 2: Internal**
What is not meant to leave the building. Project plans, meeting records. They belong only in a workflow approved for this purpose and data class.

**Level 3: Confidential**
What needs more protection in business, contractual or data protection terms: unpublished figures, customer lists, supplier terms. You need a concrete approval, plus reviewed contracts, configuration, permissions and retention. A legal basis or data protection impact assessment can come on top.

**Level 4: Restricted**
What can do serious damage when lost or mishandled. Health data, payroll data, application documents, inventions before filing. General assistants are blocked by default. Processing only in an expressly approved, tightly scoped system and workflow. Passwords, API keys and other credentials belong in no prompt, whatever the level.

Your organization may name the levels differently and draw the lines elsewhere. Fine. What counts is the published policy, not the brand name.
sections.keyTakeaway: Your organization sets data class and tool approval. You check purpose, rights, contract, configuration and permissions; a product name grants nothing.

sections.title: The decision tree
sections.content:
Five questions before every input. Every time:

1. **Purpose:** What specific task should the system perform?
2. **Data and rights:** Which data types, people, copyrights, trade secrets, or contractual duties are involved?
3. **Internal classification:** Which data class does your organization's policy assign?
4. **Approval:** Is this exact product, configuration, extension set, and workflow approved for that use?
5. **Minimization:** What can you omit, anonymize, or replace with synthetic examples?

One answer missing, you enter nothing. Full stop. Then through the published approval or escalation route. A paid licence answers none of the five, and neither does an enterprise tenant or a disabled training setting.

Cautious classification lowers the risk. It replaces no legal basis, purpose limitation, authorization or contract.
sections.keyTakeaway: Purpose, data and rights, internal classification, concrete system approval, minimization. One answer missing, you stop and take the organizational route.

quiz.questionText: An employee wants to process a customer list with names and email addresses in an unapproved AI service. Which statement holds?

answerOptions.text: Business contact details are always public and usable without further checks
A paid licence is approval enough
Processing waits until purpose, legal basis, data class and the concrete tool approval are settled
Digitally stored data may not be processed by software

quiz.explanation: Names and email addresses can be personal data. Whether processing is permitted follows from purpose, legal basis, internal classification, contract, configuration and minimization. Not from the product name. Not from the price tier.

quiz.questionText: What should you do when the confidentiality level of a data item is unclear?

answerOptions.text: Pick the lowest level so work does not stall
Stop the input and use the policy or the responsible approval function
Enter the data anyway and ask IT afterwards
Stop using AI tools entirely

quiz.explanation: Cautious classification is good. An approval it is not. If the data class or the permitted workflow is unclear, you settle it first and enter afterwards.

sections.title: The exercise
sections.content:
Take the example model from the last lesson. The levels below are assumptions for a fictional company. Your policy applies, not this table.

| No. | Data item | Example level | Additional check |
|-----|-----------|---------------|------------------|
| 1 | Approved website copy | Public | Usage rights, personal data, and currency |
| 2 | Internal meeting record | Internal | Participants, topics, consent or legal basis, approved workflow |
| 3 | Quarterly revenue before publication | Confidential | Market-disclosure, secrecy, and access rules |
| 4 | Customer list with contact details | Confidential | Purpose, legal basis, processor terms, and minimization |
| 5 | Payroll record | Restricted | Expressly approved specialist systems only; no general assistants |
| 6 | Published product catalogue | Public | Rights, version, and approved use |
| 7 | Application documents | Restricted | Purpose limitation, access, retention, and effects on applicants |
| 8 | Invention description before filing | Restricted | Patent and trade-secret controls; express approval required |
| 9 | Draft press release | Internal or confidential | Content and planned publication date |
| 10 | Supplier terms | Confidential | Contractual secrecy and permissions |

Assigning a level is the easy part. Note purpose, minimization, approval and owner beside every row.
sections.keyTakeaway: The data class is one part of the decision. Purpose, rights, system approval, configuration and minimization decide whether the workflow is permitted.

sections.title: What the table shows
sections.content:
**How the example model resolves the ten rows:**

- **Public (items 1 and 6):** Already approved. You still check rights, personal data, currency and the tool rules.
- **Internal (item 2, sometimes item 9):** Stays inside the intended audience. Only the approved workflow, and out goes what the purpose does not need.
- **Confidential (items 3, 4 and 10; item 9 depending on content):** Contract, legal basis, permissions, data region, retention and configuration have to fit the purpose. "It is an enterprise product" is no argument.
- **Restricted (items 5, 7 and 8):** General assistants are blocked here. An exception needs a documented workflow reviewed on the technical and legal side.

A real policy needs more than four levels: owners, approved products and functions, prohibited data, a reporting route for incidents, a process for new cases.
sections.keyTakeaway: The level alone documents nothing. Purpose, approved system, permitted functions, owners and escalation route belong with it.

quiz.questionText: How is an invention description before a patent filing handled under the example model?

answerOptions.text: As public, because it is a technical document
As internal; an enterprise subscription is enough for processing
As confidential; every local installation is automatically permitted
As restricted; not without an expressly approved workflow, because disclosure can jeopardize patent or trade-secret protection

quiz.explanation: Uncontrolled disclosure can cost the novelty, or the trade-secret protection. The approved patent, security and data protection process decides whether a concrete use is permitted. Neither cloud nor local is automatically right.

quiz.questionText: An internal meeting record is to be summarized with AI. Which selection rule holds?

answerOptions.text: Any service is suitable if the record contains no figures
Only a workflow approved for records, the data types involved and the exact configuration; unnecessary details come out
No system is ever suitable, not even an approved one
Every local installation is automatically suitable

quiz.explanation: A record looks harmless and can carry personal, confidential or restricted content. Product, contract, recording and transcription, permissions, retention and purpose must be expressly approved. Installed locally does not mean approved.

props.title: Redact before pasting
props.scenario: Before pasting a meeting record or customer email, inspect each piece of information: Is it necessary for the purpose, covered by the approved workflow, or should it be removed? Complete two rounds; the second contains less obvious risks.
